CrowdStrike (NASDAQ:CRWD) and Docusign (NASDAQ:DOCU) represent two distinct paths within the software market, as one pursues aggressive expansion in cybersecurity while the other refocuses on broader agreement lifecycles.

CrowdStrike is a leader in endpoint security, whereas Docusign dominates the electronic signature market. Investors often compare them to determine whether the premium price of a security leader outweighs the value proposition of a workflow giant.

The case for CrowdStrike

CrowdStrike provides AI-native cybersecurity through its Falcon platform, which secures endpoints, identities, and data for enterprises and governments. The company relies on Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) as a key third-party data center provider to deliver its cloud-based services. In its latest annual report, the company noted that it has focused on rebuilding customer trust following a major content configuration incident in mid-2024 while expanding into tech stocks related to artificial intelligence initiatives.

In FY 2026, revenue reached nearly $4.8 billion, representing growth of approximately 21.7% over the previous year. Despite this top-line expansion, the company reported a net loss of roughly $162.5 million for the period. This resulted in a net margin of -3.4%, reflecting a shift from the nominal net loss in the prior fiscal year as the company continues to invest in platform scale.

As of its January 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.2x. This ratio measures total debt relative to the value provided by shareholders. The current ratio, which measures a company's ability to cover its short-term bills with its short-term assets, is close to 1.8x. Free cash flow reached nearly $1.3 billion, though stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 68% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation because SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

The case for Docusign

Docusign has shifted its focus toward the Intelligent Agreement Management (IAM) platform, which helps organizations manage the entire lifecycle of a contract. The company serves over 1.8 million customers and maintains strategic partnerships with leaders like Salesforce (NYSE:CRM), Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT), SAP (NYSE:SAP), ServiceNow (NYSE:NOW), and Workday (NASDAQ:WDAY). It also integrates with platforms owned by Alphabet to ensure its tools are accessible within standard office workflows.

In FY 2026, revenue reached approximately $3.2 billion, an increase of about 8.2% from the prior year. The company reported net income of roughly $309.1 million, resulting in a net margin of approximately 9.6%. Although this net margin is lower than in the previous fiscal year, the company remains consistently profitable as it transitions users to its new IAM products.

Amazon (AMZN) jumped 5% to $263 after Morgan Stanley named it a top pick, with 59 analysts holding zero sell ratings and a consensus target near $331.

Morgan Stanley's Brian Nowak argues AWS growth and profit potential remain underappreciated, with a $496B backlog and 37% quarterly growth representing its fastest pace in 18 quarters.

Amazon's planned $200B capex and negative free cash flow are the key risks, though even the bear case price of $283 sits above today's level.

AWS Acceleration Pushed Amazon Back Toward Its Highs

Over the past week the stock is up 0.2%. It has gained 6.91% over the past month, 13.92% year to date and 22.61% over the past year. That leaves it 8.4% below its 52-week high of $287.20 and well above the $196 low.

In Q2, revenue grew 19.6% to $200.61 billion, beating estimates by 2.12%. GAAP EPS came in at $5.75, lifted by a $53.4 billion one-time gain tied largely to Anthropic. Comparable EPS was about $1.88 against a $1.83 estimate. AWS grew 37% to $42.23 billion, its fastest pace in 18 quarters. For Q3, management guided net sales to $197 billion to $202 billion.

Why Bulls See $378 and Beyond

The AWS backlog stands at $496 billion and is growing by triple digits. Amazon's chief executive said AWS "will be at least double that and very possibly be a trillion-dollar annual revenue business for us in time." Amazon's AI and chips businesses each run above $25 billion a year, and management is exploring selling Trainium chips outside AWS.
